title: Beef Fajitas
subtitle: Sizzling ribeye steak strips with peppers and warm tortillas
excerpt: Thinly sliced ribeye steak marinated in cumin, smoked paprika, and lime, cooked fast in a very hot pan with peppers and onion, served sizzling in warm flour tortillas with soured cream and guacamole.
sourceNotes: Beef fajitas: a Tex-Mex dish developed in southern Texas and northern Mexico in the 1930s-40s, originally made with beef skirt (arrachera) by Mexican ranch workers who received it as part of their pay. Ribeye is used here as the closest widely-available UK substitute for skirt steak.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Marinate the steak up to 24 hours ahead and keep refrigerated. Cook just before serving; fajitas go tough and dry when reheated.

content.text: Beef fajitas depend on two things: a very hot pan and slicing the meat against the grain. The steak needs high heat to sear quickly without stewing; if the pan isn't hot enough, the meat gives up its juices and steams. Slicing against the grain cuts across the muscle fibres and produces tender strips rather than chewy ones. Rest the steak for at least 5 minutes after cooking, then slice.

items.prepNote: two ribeye steaks, about 1.5 cm thick; substitute for beef skirt, which is not widely available in the UK
divided: half for the marinade, half for cooking
mashed with lime juice and salt

content.text: Marinate the steak for at least 30 minutes at room temperature or up to 24 hours in the fridge. The lime juice tenderises the meat slightly; longer than 24 hours begins to alter the texture.

Mix the cumin, smoked paprika, chilli powder, half the oil, lime juice, and salt into a paste. Coat both ribeye steaks in the mixture. Leave to marinate for at least 30 minutes, or refrigerate overnight.

Heat a large frying pan or second pan over medium-high heat with the remaining oil. Add the sliced onions and cook for 5 minutes. Add the peppers and cook for a further 5-7 minutes until soft and charred at the edges. Season with salt. Keep warm.

Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until very hot and just starting to smoke. Lay the steaks in. Cook for 2.5-3 minutes on each side for medium (adjust for thickness). Rest on a board for 5 minutes.

Slice the steak thinly against the grain and pile onto the peppers, or serve the steak and peppers in separate piles on a board. Warm the tortillas in a dry pan or microwave. Serve everything together with soured cream, mashed avocado, coriander, and jalapeño.

items.cause: Sliced with the grain rather than against it, or not rested before slicing
items.fix: Identify the grain direction of the steak (the lines of muscle fibres). Slice perpendicular to those lines, not parallel. Rest for 5 minutes before cutting.

items.symptom: Pan fills with liquid and steak steams rather than sears
items.cause: Marinade too wet, or pan not hot enough
items.fix: Pat excess marinade off the steak before it goes into the pan. The pan must be very hot. Cast iron is ideal. A crowded pan drops temperature fast; cook one steak at a time if needed.

items.symptom: Peppers are raw when the steak is done
items.cause: Peppers started at the same time as the steak
items.fix: Cook the peppers first; they take 10-12 minutes. Keep them warm in a low oven while the steak cooks.

items.cause: Steak overcooked, or soured cream and guacamole not added
items.fix: Keep the steak to medium. The cold toppings add moisture; be generous with soured cream and mashed avocado.

content.text: Fajitas originated in the ranch lands of southern Texas and northern Mexico, where Mexican vaqueros (cowboys) received beef skirt as part of their wages. It was an inexpensive cut that responded well to high-heat cooking and was served with tortillas, peppers, and onions. The dish entered American restaurant culture in the early 1980s and became a Tex-Mex staple. In the UK, ribeye is the best substitute for the traditional skirt; it has a similar fat content and takes high heat well.
